hops.afterHeading: Explore: heal a scrape, one cell at a time
hops.title: Watch a dot ride out on your fingernail
hops.text: No microscope needed. With a grown-up's okay, put a tiny dot of washable marker on a fingernail, by the skin at its base, and trace over it before it fades. Under that skin, cells keep dividing and pushing the nail forward. Measure the dot's distance from the skin now and in four weeks. In one study, young adults' fingernails grew about 3.5 millimetres a month. Pinkies were the slowpokes.

sources.citation: Yaemsiri S, Hou N, Slining MM, He K. Growth rate of human fingernails and toenails in healthy American young adults. J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 24(4):420-423, 2010

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A young person at a kitchen table, seen from behind, studies a blue dot on a fingernail while a cat leans in to look and a ruler lies nearby.
image.caption: Cells dividing at the base of your nail push it forward, and a marker dot rides along.

hops.title: Do you get a brand-new body every seven years?
hops.text: Heard your whole body gets replaced every seven years? It doesn't work that way. Different cells are replaced on different schedules, by other cells dividing. Many cells lining your gut are replaced about every three and a half days. Your outer skin renews in about 40 days. But the cells in the center of each eye's lens formed before you were born, and they stay for life.

sources.citation: Darwich AS, Aslam U, Ashcroft DM, Rostami-Hodjegan A. Meta-analysis of the turnover of intestinal epithelia in preclinical animal species and humans. Drug Metab Dispos 42(12):2016-2022, 2014
Weinstein GD, McCullough JL, Ross P. Cell proliferation in normal epidermis. J Invest Dermatol 82(6):623-628, 1984
Schey KL et al. Spatiotemporal changes in the human lens proteome: critical insights into long-lived proteins. Prog Retin Eye Res 76:100802, 2020

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A person seen from behind brushes their teeth while the mirror shows tiny cartoon cells, one leaving with a suitcase, one just arriving, and two knitting in rocking chairs.
image.caption: Your body replaces some cells every few days, and keeps others for life.

hops.afterHeading: Explain: spotting the four stages of mitosis
hops.title: The mixed-up rinse that fixed our chromosome count
hops.text: For 33 years, at least 40 studies counted 48 human chromosomes. On their slides, the coiled chromosomes of dividing cells overlapped in heaps. In 1952, T. C. Hsu reported a lucky accident: his cells were rinsed in a liquid too low in salt, which spread the chromosomes apart. Even Hsu still miscounted. Joe Hin Tjio and Albert Levan adapted the rinse, added other tricks, and in 1956 reported 46.

sources.citation: Ferguson-Smith MA. History and evolution of cytogenetics. Molecular Cytogenetics 8:19, 2015
Hogan AJ. The 'morbid anatomy' of the human genome: tracing the observational and representational approaches of postwar genetics and biomedicine. Medical History 58(3):315-336, 2014
Tjio JH, Levan A. The chromosome number of man. Hereditas 42:1-6, 1956

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A 1950s microscope and a bottle of clear rinse on a lab bench, with a round view through the eyepiece showing dark chromosomes spread neatly apart.
image.caption: A low-salt rinse spread chromosomes apart so scientists could count 46.

audio.title: A one-chromosome ant, a 35-year thumbnail and the cells you make today
audio.transcript:
Here are three true stories about cells that make more cells. Every one of them follows the rule from this lesson: copy first, then share.

Story one is about counting. A typical human body cell with a nucleus has forty-six chromosomes. That sounds like a lot to copy. Now meet two record holders. In Australia there is a bulldog ant whose males can carry just one chromosome in each cell. One. At the other end, some plants of a small fern called adder's-tongue carry about one thousand four hundred forty chromosomes. That is the highest count known for any fern.

So here is a fair question. When that fern grows, do its dividing cells get a shortcut? Nope. A growing cell copies all fourteen hundred and forty chromosomes in interphase, and in mitosis it hands one copy of each to each new cell. A growing cell in the one-chromosome ant does the same job with just one. One, forty-six or fourteen hundred and forty, the rule does not change.

Story two is about a very patient doctor. His name was William Bean, and he was curious about how fast nails grow. So he measured his own left thumbnail. He started when he was thirty-two years old, and he kept going for thirty-five years. At the start, his thumbnail grew about zero point one two millimetres a day. By the time he was sixty-seven, it had slowed to a little under zero point one. That is slow. A change that small is easier to see over weeks than from one day to the next. The growing comes from cells dividing under the skin at the base of the nail. Each new batch of cells pushes the nail forward a tiny bit. Doctor Bean watched that happen for most of his adult life. Thirty-five years, one thumbnail. That is dedication.

Story three is about you, right now. Two scientists in Israel, Ron Sender and Ron Milo, yes, two Rons, added up how many cells a typical young man's body replaces every day. For each major kind of cell, they used two clues: how many there are and how long they usually last. Their answer was about three hundred thirty billion cells a day. That works out to nearly four million every second. Close to nine out of ten of those new cells are blood cells, and most of them are made in the spongy marrow inside your bones.

Here is the twist. In your bone marrow, cells copy their chromosomes and divide to make the cells that will become red blood cells. As one of those cells matures, it stops dividing and pushes out its nucleus, chromosomes and all. So a finished red blood cell cannot divide. Every new one starts with that copying and dividing in the marrow. That is a lot of copying going on while you sit and listen.

So the next time you trim your nails, or a scrape slowly fills in with new skin, remember the cells underneath doing the same two steps, over and over: copy every chromosome, then split into two.
